asSun.p: Mars rules Aries, and The Emperor is Aries's card, so with an Aries Sun this one comes with the chart. Have a look at his throne. There are rams' heads carved into the stone at the corners, which is about as plain a signature as the deck ever gives you. The Sun's own sign is Leo. Aries is where it's exalted, which in the old language makes it an honoured guest, the planet at its most idealised, all first light and clean starts, and I think that's why Aries Suns tend to carry a picture of who they're meant to be that's a size bigger than life. Aries is cardinal fire too. Cardinal signs begin things, and fire wants them begun this afternoon. The Emperor is that same urge once it's sat down and decided to stay put for a while. For an Aries Sun that's the hard part, and usually the part you're proudest of when you manage it.

You get restless in any room where nobody is making the call. The meeting that's gone forty minutes without a decision. The group chat trying to pick a restaurant for eight people. The family dinner where everyone circles round what to do about your nan's house and nobody says it. At some point you just say it. 'Thursday, the Thai place, I'll book.' Half the time people are relieved, and the other half they're a bit put out, and you tend to notice that later, usually in the car on the way home. You also keep a quiet tally of the things you started. The netball team, the business, the Boxing Day swim that's now a tradition. With the Sun exalted here you need something to found, and a long stretch of only keeping things ticking over makes you ratty in a way you can't always explain.

Everyone mentions the leadership, so I won't. What people miss is how cleanly you own a bad call. When the thing you decided goes wrong, the booking, the hire, the move interstate, you don't hunt round for someone to share it with. You say 'that was me', you work out the next step, and you're already doing it by the time other people have finished being upset. That's rarer than it should be, and it makes you easy to follow, because people know the weight won't get passed back down to them. You can also start again from nothing, which a lot of people can't. A business folds, a relationship ends, a plan dies before it's properly begun, and after a short, loud few days you're sketching the next one on the back of an envelope and ringing someone to tell them about it.

The trouble with carrying an idealised picture of yourself is that you hate being a beginner at anything. You'll give up the pottery class after two weeks because you're bad at it and someone else in the room isn't. You'll find a reason not to go to the tennis club where you'd be the worst player. At work, being coached by someone younger, or told how to do a thing you've done your own way for years, can make you go stiff and polite and secretly furious. So the list of things you're good at stays shorter than it could be, because you only really let yourself try the ones where you're in charge from day one. It's pride, to be honest, the Aries kind, fast and a bit childish. You'd spot it in a friend inside a minute.

When something goes badly wrong your first move is to take command of it. A parent in hospital, the redundancy letter, the flooded kitchen, and inside an hour you've got a list, a plan and three phone calls made. That part works. By the following week the cost starts to show. You're short with anyone slower than you, you pick at your partner over how they stacked the dishwasher, and you won't admit you're tired, because an Aries Sun takes being seen to cope as a point of pride. The people around you start feeling like staff. They've been handed jobs and nobody's asked how they are, and they don't want to add to your load, so they go quiet. The thing that helps most is someone who'll tell you plainly that you've done enough, and then a day where every decision, dinner, the route, the film, gets made by somebody else.

You go after what you want, and in love that usually means you make the first move and make it plainly. Fine. What people don't see coming is how you show care once you're in it, which is by taking things off your partner's plate. You book the car in. You sort their tax. You've rung the landlord before they finished telling you about the leak. To you that's devotion. To them it can feel like being run, especially if they didn't ask. Libra is the sign opposite Aries, and its card is Justice, the one holding the scales. The partners who last with an Aries Sun usually bring some of that, and at some point they'll say 'that isn't fair', and they'll be right. Ask 'do you want me to handle it?' before you handle it, and wait for the answer.

You need your own patch. It can be small, one project, one shop, one team of three, but it has to be yours to decide on, and a job made entirely of carrying out other people's decisions wears you down fast. You're at your best in the founding stretch of anything. The first year of the business, the new department, the rescue job on a failing account. Once it's all running smoothly you start looking at the door, which isn't a flaw exactly, but it's worth knowing so you don't mistake boredom for failure. A boss who checks every detail gets the worst of you, and one who hands you the goal and leaves you to it gets a loyalty they probably didn't expect. If you do end up leading a big outfit, hire someone who loves the maintenance, pay them well, and let them tell you no now and then.

At twenty an Aries Sun with this card usually charges. You start five things, finish two, fall out with a manager, and you're convinced you'd run the place better, which is sometimes true. You want to be seen as the one who did it first. By the mid-thirties a lot of people with this pattern have actually built something, a business, a household, a reputation, and the new lesson is staying with it once the exciting part is over. That's when the Emperor side of the card really comes in. The fifties tend to change what being in charge means. You do less of it yourself and hand the keys to someone younger, and then you have to watch them do it differently. Some manage that gracefully. The ones who can't tend to hover, and they're usually told so, fairly bluntly, by the person they handed it to.

Next time a group decision comes up, at work or in the family, don't give your call until three other people have spoken. Count them if you have to. Then say what you think, and add one thing someone else said that changed it, even slightly. It'll feel slow and a bit maddening. Do it twice this week and notice who talks more the second time.

asMoon.p: The Moon has no special dignity in Aries. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, and like most visitors it picks up the habits of the house, and this house belongs to Mars. So your feelings arrive the way Mars does things. Quickly, hot, and wanting to do something about themselves straight away. The Emperor is Aries's card, which is why it's yours. Read as a Moon card he's about how you handle your own moods, and a lot of the time the answer is by getting up and doing something. Cardinal fire is the urge to start, and a cardinal fire Moon wants to start fixing a feeling the second it turns up. Look at how he sits on that throne, completely still. Most Aries Moons I've seen take years to learn to sit with a feeling like that for even a minute before they act on it.

Feelings come out of you as action. After an argument you're cleaning the oven at eleven at night, or you've gone for a walk that turned into a run. Anger usually gets there first, and the hurt or the fear shows up an hour behind it, which confuses people, because by then you've moved on and they're still dealing with the anger. If a friend's reply comes back as one word, 'fine', you don't wait to find out what it means. You ring. A long weekend with nothing on has you twitchy by the Saturday afternoon, so you invent a project, the shed, the spare room, a recipe that needs three shops. You're over most fights in an afternoon and genuinely puzzled when someone is still upset about it on Tuesday. And you sleep badly when something's unresolved, because your body treats it as unfinished business.

You don't hold grudges. Mars is quick in and quick out, and with the Moon in its sign you say the hard thing, have the row, and twenty minutes later you're asking what they want for dinner, and meaning it. People who grew up in families where fights went underground for weeks find that almost shocking at first, and then very restful. There's courage in how you feel, too. When a friend's marriage falls apart you're in the car before they've finished the sentence, and you'll say the thing everyone else is tiptoeing round, 'he was never kind to you', out loud. Sometimes that's exactly what they needed someone to say. You feel things clearly and act on them, so the people who love you usually know where they stand with you by the end of the day.

Anger is the feeling you're most comfortable with, so it stands in for the ones you aren't. You're scared about your dad's test results, and what comes out is a go at your partner for leaving the back door unlocked. You're sad a friendship has drifted, and what comes out is irritation at the friend. Nobody around you gets told about the fear or the sadness. They just get the heat, and they take it personally, which is fair enough from where they're standing. Slow feelings frighten you as well. Grief that won't be fixed, a low patch with no cause, missing someone. You can't organise your way through those, and you'll pick a small fight just to feel something with a clear shape to it. If you catch yourself spoiling for an argument, ask what else is going on first.

The first thing you do is move. Someone dies, a relationship ends, the diagnosis is bad, and you're organising the flowers, ringing the relatives, filling the freezer. It's useful, and people are grateful, and it's also a way of not feeling it yet. Somewhere in the second week it leaks out sideways. Short temper in traffic, snapping at the kids over shoes, lying awake at three going over what you should have done. The household ends up tiptoeing, because you seem fine and furious at the same time. What actually helps is hard exercise with nobody talking to you, a run, a swim, an afternoon digging, and then someone steady who'll let you be angry at the situation without taking it as aimed at them. The crying usually comes after that, quite fast, and it's over quicker than you feared. Let it come.

You need a partner who can take some heat without either leaving the room or firing back twice as hard. Rows happen with you. They're quick and they clear the air, and what you need from the other person is to stay put through the first five minutes. You also need to feel wanted in an active way. Chased a bit, even years in. A partner who's lovely and steady but never makes the first move can leave you oddly lonely inside a good relationship. What surprises people is that you need room to go off on your own as well. Ten minutes in the garden after an argument, a weekend away with friends, and then back, fully back. Explain that early. Someone who reads your storming off as abandonment will get it wrong every time.

At work your feelings show up as impatience, and it's worth knowing that about yourself. Long approval chains, meetings that decide to have another meeting, a colleague who takes a week to answer an email. It sits in your stomach and you can feel your mood dropping by mid-afternoon. You're very good in a crisis, though. The server's down, the client's furious, the venue has cancelled, and a crisis finally gives the feeling somewhere to go. You probably need work with some pace in it, or some physical part to it, or at least one task each day you can finish and tick off. When you're frustrated with someone at work, say so early and plainly, in private. Holding it in for a month and then saying it all at once is how an Aries Moon loses a good job.

In your twenties this Moon tends to run hot. Doors get slammed, crushes arrive and burn out inside a month, and you say things in a row you'd give a lot to take back. You move house a lot, or you want to. Through the thirties most people with this placement learn the gap, the second between the flare and the act, and that small gap changes almost everything. The home you make around then usually has plenty of noise in it and very little sulking. By the fifties the temper has mostly burnt down to a directness people come to rely on. You're still the one who'll tell a friend the truth, you've just learnt to let them finish first. The risk later on is bossing the grown children, or the ageing parents, because worrying about them feels unbearable and running their lives feels like doing something about it.

The next time you feel the flare, before you send the message or say the thing, go and put the kettle on and stay in the kitchen until it boils. Leave your phone where it is while you wait. Then write down the feeling underneath the anger in one word, on whatever's to hand. Scared, sad, embarrassed, left out. After that, decide what to do. Most days you'll still say something, just a better version of it.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is whichever sign was coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born, and it sets your first house, the body, the way you carry yourself, the way you begin. The first is Aries's own natural house, so with Aries rising the sign is sitting exactly where it's most at home, which is why it shows so plainly. It also makes Mars your chart ruler, so wherever Mars sits in your chart is one of the most important things about you, and worth looking up if you haven't. Aries is cardinal fire, the sign that starts things, and on the Ascendant it comes out as speed, the sense that you've already begun. The Emperor is Aries's card, so he's the one strangers meet at the door. Look closely and there's armour showing under his red robe, on his legs, and people meeting you tend to sense something like it before you've said much.

It starts with the walk. Aries rising usually moves fast and leads with the head, first through the door, first to the counter, a bit ahead of whoever you're walking with. In a room full of strangers you're often the first to speak, and at a new job you've introduced yourself to the manager's manager by the end of week one. When the train stops between stations and nobody knows why, you're the one who goes to find out. Strangers ask you for directions. People you've known for ten minutes ask what you think they should do, and you tell them. You also interrupt, and you know it. And you size up a room quickly, who's in charge, where the exits are, who's going to be difficult, before you've taken your coat off.

You make it easy for shy people to follow you. Plenty of people would like to do the brave thing and can't go first, and you go first without a second thought, so they can come second. The school fundraiser that needed someone to stand up, the neighbourhood meeting about the development, the first person on the dance floor at your cousin's wedding. It's you when something frightening happens in public, too. Someone collapses at the station and you're already kneeling down, pointing at a stranger and telling them to ring triple zero. You aren't fearless. Mars at the front of the chart gets the body moving before the fear has caught up, and in the first minute of anything bad that counts for a great deal. People remember it about you for years.

Your concentrating face reads as cross. You're just thinking, working out the next step, and the person across the desk decides you're annoyed with them. Aries rising gets into a lot of arguments it didn't mean to start, simply because the tone arrives before the meaning does. At a service desk, asking a perfectly reasonable question, you can come across much harsher than you felt. You'll also pick up fights on behalf of the room. Someone's being treated unfairly in a meeting and you're the one who says so, sharply, and then somehow you're the one who looks aggressive while everyone else looks reasonable. That happens a lot. It's worth softening the delivery even when you're right, and especially then. Starting with the person's name, or with a question, takes a lot of the edge off the same point.

Stress shows on you straight away, in the face and the voice, before you've decided how you feel about anything. A crisis at work, a family emergency, a bad week with a sick kid, and you get faster and sharper, and people who don't know you well assume you're angry with them. Some of them step back. Others push back, and now there are two problems. A few days in it moves into the body. You bang your shin on the coffee table, burn your hand on the oven tray, drive a bit too fast on the way to the hospital. Mars rules your chart and the first house is the body, so the body takes the knocks. Slowing yourself down on purpose is what helps. A long bath, a slow walk, a meal eaten sitting at the table. And somebody asking 'what do you need from me?', then doing exactly that and nothing extra.

With Aries on the first house, Libra lands on your seventh, the house of partners. So the people you're drawn to tend to be charming, fair-minded, a bit diplomatic, the sort who ask what you'd like before they say what they want. They slow you down. They also soften how you come across, and you probably know that and quietly rely on it at parties. In the first few weeks the front you lead with can put gentler people off before they've got to know you, so it's worth letting them see you laugh, and letting them pick where you go. Cancer sits on your fourth house, home, and what goes on behind your front door is much softer than anyone would guess from the handshake. A partner is one of the few who gets to see that.

With Aries rising, Capricorn falls on your tenth house, career and reputation. Capricorn squares Aries, both cardinal, one fire and one earth, so there's friction built in. You come across as quick and bold, and the career that suits you is built slowly, one rung and one decade at a time. The authority that sticks is the kind you've earned by being reliable for years. You tend to get hired for your decisiveness, because people like the straight answers in an interview. The real test comes after, in whether you'll stay the course in a place with a hierarchy. Pushing too fast in an institution that moves slowly can burn bridges you'd want later. Pick your battles with senior people, wait your turn longer than feels natural, and keep a record of what you've delivered, because in the end it's the record that gets you promoted.

At twenty Aries rising is all momentum. You're taken for older and surer of yourself than you are, you get handed responsibility early, and you jump into things head first, jobs, cities, relationships. Plenty of bruises, literal and otherwise. Through the thirties the Capricorn tenth house starts paying. The reputation you've built by turning up and getting it done begins to count, and people offer you the job before you ask. The front calms down a bit as well. You learn to walk into a room without having to take it. By the fifties the quickness usually settles into bearing, and people describe you as someone with presence. The body needs more looking after than it did in your twenties, and the Mars pace doesn't always suit it, so it's worth listening when your knees or your back have an opinion.

For one day this week, walk slower than you normally would. Everywhere. To the car, down the corridor, into the meeting. Before you go through the door of any room with strangers in it, stop for a breath, drop your shoulders and let your face go soft, the way it is when you're reading something you like. Then go in. Notice who comes up to you that day who usually wouldn't. The slow walking will probably be driving you mad by lunchtime. Keep going anyway.

asBirthCard.p: This one comes from your birthdate, and your signs have nothing to do with it. Add up every digit, and if the total goes over 22 add those digits again. Totals of 4, 31 or 40 all land on four, and four is The Emperor. Four is two twice over. It's the number of corners on a square and legs on a table, the first number you can build with that stands up on its own. In the sequence of Majors, The Empress comes right before him, and she grows things. The Emperor comes next and puts a fence round what's grown so it lasts. After him comes The Hierophant, who takes the rules and teaches them to others. The card's own sign is Aries, cardinal fire, so the four in this deck has some hurry in it, and gets impatient when the building stalls.

Over a lifetime, four shows up as being the one who makes things run. Not always in charge, but the one holding it together. In a share house you're the one who ended up doing the bills spreadsheet. When a relative dies you're the one on the phone to the funeral home and the bank, and you've made a folder. At work you're the person who noticed the roster didn't add up and quietly rebuilt it. When friends go camping, you're the one who packed the first aid kit, and you're mildly annoyed that nobody else did. You probably keep routines, the same breakfast, the same Sunday, the same order for doing the shopping, and they aren't boring to you. They're what lets everything else happen. When your routine goes, you feel it straight away.

Things you set up keep working after you've walked away, and that's the part people don't see at the time. The committee you chaired has a process that still runs ten years on. The savings plan you set up for your niece is still quietly paying in. The weekly dinner you started with your siblings is still going, even the year two of you weren't talking. Four is the number of foundations, and foundations don't get thanked, because when they do their job nobody looks at them. You also keep your word, and over the years that adds up to something unusual. Your friends' kids know that if you said you'd be at the recital, you'll be there, third row, a few minutes early.

Once you've built a thing, it's hard for you to leave it, even after it's stopped working for you. The job you created the systems for. The club you've been treasurer of for twelve years. A relationship whose whole structure, the house, the routines, the way Christmas goes, was put together by you. Walking away feels like pulling down a wall you laid yourself, so you stay and keep maintaining something nobody else is using much. There's a quieter one as well. Four finds it very hard to cope with things that can't be built or fixed. Grief, an illness in the family, a child who's struggling for no clear reason. You'll respond by reorganising the house, starting a new routine, making a chart. It helps a little. Mostly it gives you somewhere to put your hands.

When things go wrong, four tightens the structure. More rules, more lists, a stricter routine, earlier alarms. It's how you get a floor back under yourself, and in the first few days it genuinely works. The trouble comes about a week in, when the routine hardens into a wall. You stop talking about how you feel because you're busy keeping things running, and you get rigid about small stuff, the dishwasher, the bedtime, the way the towels are folded. The people you live with start to feel like they're in an institution, and some of them stop telling you things. What actually helps is letting someone take one whole job off you, entirely, done their way, and loosening one rule on purpose. Then sit down with somebody and talk about the thing itself, the loss or the fear, and leave the arrangements out of it for an hour.

You show love by building. The joint account, the house deposit, the holiday booked a year out, the fixed night of the week that's just for the two of you. For you that's romance, and a partner who understands that tends to feel very safe with you. What's harder to see from the inside is that you need someone who'll help write the rules. Four is made of two and two, so a structure with you in it works best when both of you have your hands on it. If you do all the building and they just live inside it, you start to feel like the landlord. Now and then, ask a partner which of the routines they'd drop if they could. The answer might surprise you, and they may never have felt allowed to say.

You're often the second person in, the one who takes the founder's messy idea and turns it into a business that can pay its staff. Operations, finance, law, construction, project management, running a school or a ward or a warehouse. Anything where structure is what makes the good work possible. You're the one who writes the policy that saves everyone an argument later. People don't always notice the work, because when it's done well nothing goes wrong, so make sure the people above you can see it. Keep a list of what you fixed. The risk is building systems for their own sake, or for a place that will never value them, and working long unpaid hours to keep a structure standing that isn't yours. Ask whose it is before you give it your weekends.

In your twenties, four often plays out as a fight with structure. Either you cling to it, the rules, the plan, the five-year spreadsheet, or you kick against every structure anyone hands you and then build your own the hard way. By the mid-thirties most people with this card have built something that holds. A household, a team, a practice. The work then is learning to maintain it without it swallowing you, and letting it change shape when your life does. The fifties tend to bring what comes after The Emperor in the deck. You start teaching what you know, passing the systems on, being the one the younger ones ask. The ones who manage it best let the next person change what they built, and don't take it as an insult.

Pick one rule or routine you keep at home, the bedtimes, the way the kitchen gets cleaned, how money is split. Ask the people it affects, one at a time, whether it still works for them. Listen to the whole answer before you explain why it's there. Then change one thing they asked for and leave it changed for a month, even if you'd have done it differently.
